candidate.sense: edible corn kernels or an ear of corn used as food

claims.proposition: KBBI defines jagung as both the plant and its edible fruit or seeds, covering the proposed food sense.
Indonesian recipe usage includes jagung manis pipil for sweet corn kernels used as food.
Jagung denotes maize, including its edible cob and kernels.
Jagung is used for corn as a food ingredient in Malaysian recipes.
Indonesian jagung and Malaysian jagung are identical written everyday forms and commonly refer to edible corn in shopping and cooking.

context.scope: Common named fruits and vegetables in ordinary shopping and cooking; neutral single-produce cues; seek useful Indonesian and Malaysian Malay contrasts that can plausibly be evidenced in independent dictionary and grocery or recipe sources; exclude all previously investigated concepts

source_inspections.method: AI-assisted direct page inspection with web open/find

sources.observation: The jagung entry includes the edible fruit or seeds of Zea mays. The site says it is an unofficial archive based mainly on KBBI edition III; it cannot establish current preferred usage.
The Indonesian retailer's recipe discusses jagung as food and lists jagung manis that has been removed from the cob. This is contextual use, not a frequency comparison.
The Malay entry defines jagung as Zea mays and its grain. It is community-edited; the page also links to DBP but the DBP entry itself was not opened.
A contributor in Klang, Selangor uses jagung manis kernel and jagung manis krim in a Malaysian recipe. One user recipe supports contextual usage only.
sources.page_location: author location and recipe ingredients, lines 52-66 and 116-130

source_leads.exact_claim: Defines jagung as the plant and as buah atau biji jagung.
Lists jagung manis, pipil, as a soup ingredient.

source_leads.claim: Defines jagung as a plant whose cob bears edible grains, Zea mays.
Uses nasi jagung in a Malaysian recipe title and mentions jagung manis as an ingredient.

prompt:
# Audit external evidence (prompt set 1.1.0)

Independently inspect every proposed source or corpus result. A model citation, URL, or dictionary
entry by itself is only a lead. For each observation, state exactly which claim is supported,
contradicted, or left inconclusive. Record the access method, page location or reproducible query,
short observed content, access time, publisher, underlying source group, locale, register, and
limitations. Count mirrors and copied pages as one underlying source. A dictionary listing proves
existence or a sense, not normal everyday preference by itself. Report contrary evidence.
Use one underlying source per observation; never join publishers, domains, or URLs into
one record. Mark a search snippet as inconclusive, not a retrieved page. Do not invent
an access time or claim to have opened a page if only a search result was visible.
For common use, seek an independent contextual source in each locale. For an everyday
preference claim, seek comparative evidence or more than an isolated product listing.
An inaccessible lead contributes no support; it is acceptable to return fewer observations.

Return JSON only: `{"schema_version":1,"role":"evidence-audit","model":"MODEL/TOOL",
"result":{"observations":[{"evidence_id":"...","claim_id":"...","source_group":"...",
"source_title":"...","publisher":"...","url_or_query":"...","accessed_at":"ISO UTC",
"observation":"...","page_location_or_query":"...",
"audit_method":"retrieved-page|corpus-query|manual-inspection",
"stance":"supports|contradicts|inconclusive","claim_type":"meaning|locale-usage|preferred-choice|relation|misleading-contrast",
"usage_basis":"contextual|comparative|dictionary-only","locale":"...","register":"...",
"limitations":"..."}]}}`.
If a source cannot be inspected, omit it from supporting observations and report the failure.
